documentation.range:
This species has the widest distribution of the genus. It was previously known from the Atlantic slopes and lowlands from southern Veracruz and northern Oaxaca in Mexico, through Guatemala and Belize, south-east to northern Honduras, through Nicaragua and Costa Rica, continuing on to the Caribbean slope to Panama, and from an isolated record from Cartagena Botanic Garden in northern Colombia. In Costa Rica, it occurs in the whole country except in the province Heredia (Savage and Heyer 1967). It is now also present on Mancarroncito Island (Barquero 2010), and from Carozo and Estelí Departments (Sunyer et al. 2014) in Nicaragua. It has an altitudinal range from sea level up to 1,700 m asl.

The intraspecific morphological differences, suggest that this species could be three different species, one northern (from Mexico to north-west Honduras), one central (in Nicaragua and the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica), and one southern (Pacific coast of Costa Rica and Panamá; Duellman 2001), although currently these populations have not been recognized as separate.
documentation.population: This is generally considered to be an abundant species common throughout its range. Due to ongoing decline in the extent and quality of habitat, the international pet trade and disease, the population is suspected to be experiencing some local declines.
documentation.habitats: This species inhabits tropical lowland and montane forest, where there is a continuous forest cover. The presence of temporary or permanent ponds is important for its reproduction, which takes place by larval development. It can live in secondary forest, and even very heavily degraded areas as long as there is tree cover close to ponds (F. Bolaños pers. comm.).
documentation.threats: The habitat within the range of this species is under threat from deforestation and degradation from agricultural activities, urban expansion and logging. However, this species does well in areas where there has been selective logging and is considered to be fragmentation-tolerant (Bell and Donnelly 2006). Wild subpopulations in Costa Rica, Nicaragua and Panama are threatened by capture for the international pet trade (CITES 2015). Disease is also a threat, and wild tadpoles have experienced ranavirus-related die-offs (Stark et al. 2014). This species is a carrier of the amphibian chytrid fungus and was found to have moderate prevalence of Bd infection across Panama subpopulations, but all were at extremely low infection intensities (Rebolar et al. 2014).
documentation.measures: This species is found in many protected areas throughout its range. It has been listed on CITES Appendix II since 2008. In 2013-2014, the Scientific Authority of CITES in Mexico (CONABIO), in close collaboration with experts, produced an identification guide and poster to spread the knowledge of the species regulation under CITES.
documentation.use_trade: This species is very common in the pet trade and is field collected and exported for the trade, although it is commonly bred in captivity for this purpose. The predominant source of declared imported animals is captive-bred, although Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama do export live wild-caught animals for the trade (CITES 2015). It was on the list of 15 most traded amphibian species in the USA, with more than a quarter of a million traded between 2001-2009 (Herrel and van der Meijden 2014).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern in view of its wide distribution, tolerance of a degree of habitat modification and presumed large population.
